previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis likely due to underlying vasculitis, was readmitted for recurrent abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting just three days after a prior discharge. She had not tolerated oral prednisone, which exacerbated her nausea. During this admission, she was managed supportively with NPO status, IV fluids, and IV Dilaudid for pain. Her PPI was switched to IV famotidine due to an allergy to IV pantoprazole, and prednisone was discontinued. Her symptoms improved over 72 hours, she advanced to a regular diet, and her medications were transitioned back to oral form. A urine culture suggested possible contamination, but a short course of Macrobid was prescribed as a precaution. She received parenteral nutrition before discharge. The patient was discharged home in good condition, with pain controlled and oral intake tolerated, and instructed to follow up with her specialist to address long-term management of her vasculitis and prevent recurrent admissions.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified

Brief Hospital Course:
___ female with chronic pancreatitis was admitted with 
recurrent abdominal pain consistent with her typical flares of 
chronic pancreatitis. 

* Abdominal Pain/Chronic Pancreatitis: Pain was similar to her 
previous pancreatitis pain, for which she has been admitted 
multiple times over the last few months.  She was kept NPO with 
IVF.  However, her blood work, as well as RUQ U/S could not 
demonstrate a clear cause of her pain.  Prior images were 
reviewed, not entirely consistent with pancreatitis.  Given her 
history of possible vasculitis, rheumatology was consulted.  
Psychiatry was consulted as well to assess for for conversion 
disorder as a possible contribution to her pain.  The case was 
also discussed with her ___ Dr. ___, as well as 
her surgeon, Dr. ___, with no clear etiology.  The 
rheumatologists did not feel that her symptoms were consistent 
with a vasculitis.  RNP, anti- Ro/La, IgG sublcass, and 
cryoglobulins were tested and pending at discharge.  They also 
recommended repeating a salivary gland biospy as an outpatient, 
as well as considering Evoxac.  Her methotrexate will also need 
to be discussed with her rheumatologist.  Psychiatry had 
evaluated her and felt that they could not rule in or out the 
possibility of conversion disorder.  They recommended checking 
TSH, which was wnl and also to consider initiating mirtazepine 
(and discontinuing amitryptilline).  This change was not 
initiated in house and will defer to outpatient therapist and 
PMD regarding this decision. An attempt was made to contact her 
outpatient therapist, but unable to directly speak with the 
therapist.  Ultimately, will need outpatient follow up with her 
PMD and therapist.  ON the day of discharge, she was able to 
tolerate regular diet and her pain was well controlled on PO 
dilaudid.

* Hematemesis: On admission to the hospital the patient had 20ml 
of hematemesis after an episode of wretching.  The episode was 
not witnessed by was examined by the nocturnist, which was 
described as BRB without gastric contents.  She then had a 
second episode 1 day later.  Hct remained stable/increased 
throughout.  Case was discussed with GI, and given this had 
happened before 3 weeks ago, for which she underwent EGD which 
was grossly normal (except for esophagitis on biopsy), the 
etiology was presumed to ___ tear from persistent 
wretching.  Her Hct remained stable throughout her 
hospitalization.

* Orthostatic Hypotension: Continued betaxolol and florinef once 
she was able to tolerate orals.

* Depression and Anxiety: Continued lexapro and amitryptiline 
once able to tolerate PO.

* Esophagitis: Continued pantoprazole 40mg PO BID for her active 
gastritis.

* Vasculitis: As discussed above.  Per rheumatology, unlikely to 
be vasculitis.  Multiple serologies pending (listed above).  
Continued methotrexate should be discussed with her 
rheumatologist.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted with recurrent abdominal pain.  You were given 
IV fluids, analgesics, and nausea medication.  Though you had 
episodes of bloody wretching, your hematocrit was stable, which 
was likely related to your vomiting.  The psychiatrists and 
rheumatologists evaluated you as well.  The rheumatologists did 
not think you have an active vasculitis.  Blood work was drawn 
to investigate this, for which follow up with your 
rheumatologist will be necessary.  You have a follow up 
appointment with your primary gastroeneterologist tomorrow, 
which you should attend.

Please take all home medications as before.  Resume your diet 
slowly.  Discuss with your rheumatologist regarding continuing 
your methotrexate.

are not able to tolerate orals.
